introduction.text: Santa Maria in Trastevere is a church on the piazza of the same name in Rome's Trastevere district. Largely rebuilt under Pope Innocent II in the twelfth century, it has a central nave separated from its side aisles by 22 ancient granite columns, thought to have come from the Baths of Caracalla. The Romanesque bell tower and the façade restored by Carlo Fontana form part of its exterior. Inside, medieval mosaics above the altar include Innocent II holding a model of the church, with Pietro Cavallini's scenes from the Life of the Virgin below. Domenichino's painting of the Assumption sits within a wooden coffered ceiling. The Altemps Chapel houses the early medieval Madonna della Clemenza, while in Antonio Gherardi's Avila Chapel hidden windows illuminate a chamber above the dome.

history.description: Pope Innocent II rebuilt the church on its earlier foundations between 1140 and 1143.
Tradition links the site's earliest church to Pope Callixtus I, but the beginnings of Christian worship here remain uncertain.

design.description: The 22 ancient granite columns divide the central nave from the side aisles. They are thought to have come from the Baths of Caracalla.

In the Avila Chapel, Antonio Gherardi used windows hidden from below to illuminate a chamber above the dome. Four small sculpted figures seem to carry a miniature temple within the opening, turning light into part of the architecture.
The Romanesque bell tower dates from the twelfth century. Carlo Fontana restored the façade in 1702; a balustrade with statues of four popes stands above it.

art.description: The twelfth-century mosaic above the altar includes Pope Innocent II holding a model of the church. Below it, Pietro Cavallini's mosaics from 1291 show episodes from the Life of the Virgin.
emphasis: holding a model of the church

art.description: The Altemps Chapel holds the Madonna della Clemenza, a painted image of the Virgin and Child dated between the sixth and ninth centuries.
Domenichino painted the Assumption of the Virgin in 1617. The octagonal painting sits within the wooden coffered ceiling that he also designed.
